cards.explanation: The answer is that he cheers for him as king. Hushai, David's friend, walks up and says, “Long live the king! Long live the king!” He says it TWICE, friends. David had sent him back to the city for exactly this kind of moment (2 Samuel 15:32-34). I bet he figured two cheers beat one.

The answer is that Absalom asks why Hushai didn't go with David. Absalom, David's son, says, “Is this the loyalty you show your friend?” and then, “Why did you not go with your friend?” He's poking at Hushai's loyalty. That's a tough question to get when you've just walked in cheering.

The answer is True. Hushai says, “As I served in your father’s presence, so also I will serve in yours.” He answers Absalom's question with a question of his own: “…whom should I serve if not his son?” I think that's a smooth answer.

The answer is that it will strengthen everyone on Absalom's side. Ahithophel says that when all Israel hears Absalom has become a stench to his father, “…then the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened.” His advice is heavy, and I think this is a hard part of the story. But the text is clear about what he says it will do.

The answer is that they regarded it like consulting the word of God. The writer says Ahithophel's advice “…was like the consultation of the word of God,” and both David and Absalom thought so. When your advice gets treated like that, you're a big deal. I can't even get bakers to trust my oven timer.

The answer is False. Ahithophel says, “Let me choose twelve thousand men and set out tonight in pursuit of David.” He's not waiting a few weeks, he's going TONIGHT. This man doesn't even want to sleep on it.
The word is king. Ahithophel says, “I will strike down only the king…” After he throws David into a panic and the people flee, that's his target. It's a plan aimed at one man.

The word is peace. Ahithophel says, “You seek the life of only one man; then all the people will be at peace.” Absalom, David's son, is after one man's life, and Ahithophel claims the rest will settle down. It's a plan that sounds neat, and that's the scary part.

The answer is False. The text says, “This proposal seemed good to Absalom and all the elders of Israel.” Not just Absalom, but the elders too. When Absalom and the elders both like it, that's a pitch that landed.

The answer is False. Hushai tells Absalom, “This time the advice of Ahithophel is not sound.” The text says Ahithophel's advice was “…like the consultation of the word of God.” (2 Samuel 16:23). I think pushing back on that takes nerve.

The answer is the troops. Hushai says David “…is a man of war who will not spend the night with the troops.” So David isn't going to be sitting in a camp where he's easy to find. That's the argument Hushai is making.
The answer is True. Hushai says, “Surely by now he is hiding in a cave or some other location.” He opens with “Surely,” and he doesn't hedge. That's a bold way to make an argument.

The word is slaughter. Hushai says whoever hears will say, “There has been a slaughter among the troops who follow Absalom.” It's a hard picture. He's describing what the news would be if some of Absalom's troops fall first.

The answer is Absalom himself. Hushai says, “I advise that all Israel from Dan to Beersheba…be gathered to you, and that you yourself lead them into battle.” Look at that, he puts Absalom, David's son, right at the front. It's a flattering plan, and Absalom likes it.

The answer is True. Hushai says, “If he retreats to a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it down to the valley until not even a pebble can be found there.” That's a big speech. He's going all in.

The name is Hushai. Absalom and all the men of Israel say, “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than that of Ahithophel.” David's friend wins the room. And remember, they started out liking Ahithophel's plan (2 Samuel 17:4).

The answer is that the LORD planned to defeat it. The text says, “For the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom.” Ahithophel's counsel was good, and the LORD purposed to thwart it. That's the real story behind the room.

The answer is to cross over and not stay the night. Hushai says, “Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but be sure to cross over.” He adds that otherwise the king and all the people with him “…will be swallowed up.” He tells them to move QUICKLY.

The answer is True, friends. The text says, “But a young man did see them and told Absalom.” Jonathan and Ahimaaz “…dared not be seen entering the city.” Somebody saw them anyway. Their quiet job just got a lot less quiet.
The word is well. The man in Bahurim “…had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it.” A well is a bold hiding place. I respect anybody willing to climb down into one.

The answer is that she covers it and scatters grain on top. The man's wife “…took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain over it so nobody would know a thing.” Cover first, then grain on top. I think that's quick thinking.
The answer is that they crossed over the brook. She tells Absalom's servants, “They have crossed over the brook…” Meanwhile the two men are down in the well. The servants search but do not find them.
The answer is False. “The men searched but did not find them, so they returned to Jerusalem.” They looked, and they came up empty. Two men down a well, and the servants went back to Jerusalem.
The word is daybreak, friends. “By daybreak, there was no one left who had not crossed the Jordan.” David and all the people with him got across. Not one person was left on the wrong side.

The answer is his house in his hometown, friends. Ahithophel “…saddled his donkey and set out for his house in his hometown.” He doesn't go back to Absalom, and he doesn't go to David. This is a heavy part of the story. I think this one hurts.
